preflight.py:162-185: the handler's `import pymysql` (line 169) runs only when _check_rule_set_catalog is reached. rule_sets.py:77-78 _Record config is extra=forbid, strict=True, frozen=True, with no aliases or validate_by_name, so the key 'value' maps directly to the field. CompareRule.value (line 204) has default None. In pydantic v2, model_fields_set holds the names of fields explicitly supplied at validation, regardless of the supplied value (0, False, '' and None all count) and excludes defaulted ones. Mode='after' validators (line 207-209) run on the constructed instance, where fields_set is already populated. Strict mode only affects type coercion, not fields_set, and frozen does not matter. Claim text is at docs/external/rule-sets.md:110. In src/sqllens/rule_sets.py, _Compiler._node (567-636) builds only positive predicates. The comparison operators are =, !=, <, <=, >, >= (_COMPARISONS, 454-456) plus IN. All of them are NULL when the column is NULL, so the row is not visible. any_of compiles to OR and all_of to AND, both monotone. inherit, referenced_by and owner_via compile to EXISTS over EQ matches, and a NULL join key never matches. There is no NOT, NOT IN, IS NULL, COALESCE or null-safe equality anywhere in the compiler. Counter-input traced: a NULL column under `!=` or `in` gives NULL, so the row is filtered out. A NULL foreign key under inherit gives no EXISTS match, so the row is filtered out. Because the compiled tree has no negation, NULL can never turn into true. I did not read the guard code that applies the condition to statements, and the claim is about the compiled condition.

In sqlglot 30.31.0 (the installed version, within the pinned >=30.22,<31) optimizer/scope.py:871-904 `_traverse_ctes` fills cte_sources only with Scope objects. For a recursive CTE the entry is scope.branch(cte.this.this) (line 884), and otherwise the last child scope yielded from scope.branch(cte.this) (888-900). Scope.expression is expression.unnest() (line 173), which strips Paren and Subquery wrappers. So expression is cte.this, its recursive base branch, or a nested set-op or select inside cte.this. Each of these is a strict descendant of the defining exp.CTE, so find_ancestor(exp.CTE) returns that CTE. Inner CTEs nested in a CTE body resolve to their own defining CTE. Outer-scope sources are inherited through cte_sources=scope.cte_sources (lines 177, 743-783) and are the same CTE-derived scopes. The direct `exp.CTE` branch at rule_sets.py:395 is never needed, and if a later sqlglot returned something else, line 396-397 raises RuleSetRefusal rather than misrenaming. _is_cte_reference (rule_sets.py:277-282) only checks that the name is in cte_sources and that db and catalog are absent, so it adds no other source type.

apply_rule_set (rule_sets.py:816-820) chooses a prefix then calls _rename_ctes whenever rules is non-empty, before _analyze/_rewrite. _choose_prefix (365-376) picks sl<n>_ so that no lowercased identifier in the whole tree (aliases, CTE names, tables, columns), no listed table and no rule table starts with it. Every alias the guard writes is <prefix><k>_<slot> (353-354) and so cannot collide with a model name, including one that does not start with 'sl<n>_' (that would not match the prefix test). k is a per-statement counter (_rewrite 590-597), so aliases are unique. _scoped_body (414-416) aliases the base table, and CompiledRule.instantiate (rules rule_sets.py:526-538) rewrites every slot alias and column qualifier to the guard aliases. _rename_ctes (379-402) renames every CTE found by find_all(exp.CTE) and every reference traverse_scope resolves. Counterexample tried: a CTE in a scope traverse_scope misses. Its definition would be renamed but its reference would not. The reference then resolves to no CTE and would be an unresolved or unaccounted table, which _analyze (298-318) refuses. Even when the name matches a listed table, the leftover table is refused as unaccounted (312-318). _rewalk re-checks after generation. So no CTE can stand in for a filter table.

rule_sets.py:365-376 _choose_prefix collects lowercased names of every exp.Identifier in the tree (find_all reaches all args, including quoted and string-literal-sourced aliases, which sqlglot parses as Identifier), plus all keys of `tables` and all rule.tables, and increments the index until no name startswith f"sl{index}_". The returned prefix is therefore not a case-insensitive prefix of any of those names, which matches the docstring at 343-346. It is called once, on the parsed tree before any rewriting (line 819), and the guard's own identifiers are written afterwards using that prefix. Non-Identifier nodes such as function names (Anonymous) or Var cannot become an alias or CTE name that collides with the guard's names. I did not find a counterexample.

rule_sets.py:701-733. For each rule table with a base alias <prefix>k_0 inside a guard-shaped wrapper (_wrapper_body, 684-698), the body is compared via _shape (425-442, full recursive structural key, all args) against a fresh _scoped_body; any difference raises RuleSetRefusal (727-730), so every table inside a proven body (collected at 732) equals a guard-built table. A repeated k raises at 722-723 (checked before seen.add at 731, so the second occurrence is refused). Falsification attempt: when _wrapper_body returns None (wrapper has alias columns, extra args, or no wrapper) or base_index is None, the table is skipped at 717-721 and not refused in this function. But there is no body to differ in that case, and the only caller (_rewalk, 752) then refuses it: the table is not in `built`, so 760-763 raises for any sourced table with a row rule, and 775-777 raises for any unaccounted table. So the claim holds for bodies the function recognizes, and the overall guard has no gap. The docstring does not mention the skip, which is only a minor imprecision.

rule_sets.py:405-422 `_scoped_body` builds SELECT cols FROM name WHERE rule LIMIT _MATERIALIZE_LIMIT (18446744073709551615), matching the docstring at 408-413. MySQL documents that a derived table containing LIMIT cannot be merged (derived_merge applies only to mergeable subqueries, and the setting can only turn merging off or allow it where it is already possible). Derived-condition pushdown (8.0.22+) is likewise not applied to derived tables with LIMIT. The connector tests back this up. test_explain_shows_scoped_tables_materialized_and_unscoped_mergeable (tests/connectors/test_row_rules_mysql.py:295-315) asserts the scoped wrappers show as DERIVED while the unscoped wrapper is merged. test_a_model_expression_never_runs_on_a_hidden_row (283-292) shows an overflow expression in the model's WHERE does not touch a hidden row. I did not run this against a live MySQL server or try a non-default optimizer_switch. I traced the optimizer rules from the MySQL docs and the test code only. No non-default setting can make a LIMIT-bearing derived table merge. I found no counterexample for the absolute wording.
